references.text: The psalmist's prophetic lament: "They gave me vinegar to drink when I was thirsty." The soldiers who offered Jesus vinegar (ὄξος) at the cross directly fulfill this messianic prophecy from [ref:Ps 69:21|Psalm 69:21].
In Matthew's account of the crucifixion, one of those present runs and fills a sponge with vinegar and gives it to Jesus to drink, paralleling the soldiers' action in [ref:Matt 27:48|Matthew 27:48].
Mark's parallel account tells how someone filled a sponge with vinegar and offered it to Jesus ([ref:Mark 15:36|Mark 15:36]).
John's account of the soldiers giving Jesus vinegar to drink at the crucifixion. John explicitly links this to the fulfillment of Scripture ([ref:John 19:28-30|John 19:28-30]).

In the verse just before, Jesus is mocked by the Jewish leaders, and the soldiers' mockery in verse 36 continues this pattern of scorn. Luke describes several groups mocking Jesus ([ref:Luke 23:35|Luke 23:35]).

Matthew recounts the soldiers' mockery of Jesus before the crucifixion, where they dressed him in a robe, placed a crown of thorns on his head, and mocked him as the king of the Jews—the same soldiers who here continue to mock him ([ref:Matt 27:27-31|Matthew 27:27-31]).

The soldiers' mockery is made concrete in the next verse where they say: "If you are the king of the Jews, save yourself!" This reveals the content of the scorn from verse 36 ([ref:Luke 23:37|Luke 23:37]).

Isaiah's prophecy about the suffering servant who was despised and rejected by people. The soldiers' mockery and scorn at the cross fulfill this prophecy concerning the Messiah's suffering and rejection ([ref:Isa 53:3|Isaiah 53:3]).

Vinegar (ὄξος) is mentioned in connection with the Nazirite vow. The term vinegar/sour wine holds a special place in biblical tradition and forms the background for the soldiers offering Jesus vinegar as an act of mockery ([ref:Num 6:3|Numbers 6:3]).
